summary: Provides a brief outline of a National Research and Education Network. It is informational and not a statement of IAB policy.

plainLanguage.summary: A short sketch of a national network for schools and researchers, with ideas on what it might be like.

subtitle: A vision for a U.S. national research and education network.

tldr.problem: The U.S. research and education community needed a unified, high-speed network to serve diverse institutions and enable collaboration.
tldr.mechanism: Cerf outlined how the NREN would evolve from the existing Internet, integrating government, commercial, and private networks with advanced technologies like FDDI, DQDB, and ATM.
tldr.outcome: The paper sketched a vision for a multi-protocol, multi-constituency network that emphasized commercial participation and federal support for institutional access, which influenced subsequent networking policy.

today: RFC 1167 is an informational RFC that sketched visions for the NREN. While the specific organizational details and technologies changed, many of Cerf's concepts influenced how the Internet evolved: federal support shifted toward institutional access through funding mechanisms; commercial providers became central to backbone infrastructure; and the multi-protocol, multi-stakeholder approach remained the norm.

sections.title: What Is the NREN?
sections.content:
The National Research and Education Network (NREN) would be a computer network serving U.S. colleges, universities, government research agencies, schools, and research organizations. Rather than building something entirely new, the NREN was intended to grow out of the existing Internet, which at the time consisted of numerous government-sponsored networks like ARPANET, NSFNET, and others.

The RFC is Vinton Cerf's personal thoughts on how such a network should be designed and operated. It does not represent official policy but rather sketches the major considerations that would shape the NREN's form and evolution.
sections.plainLanguage: The NREN is a big idea for connecting research schools and government labs across the country. Instead of starting from scratch, it would grow from the existing Internet.

sections.title: Technical Foundation
sections.content:
The NREN's technical design would rest on several fundamentals. First, it would maintain a layered network architecture with local area networks, metropolitan, regional, and wide-area networks working together. Second, it would use multiple technologies: high-speed fiber (FDDI), broadband ISDN with ATM switching, conventional Ethernet, token ring networks, X.25 packet switching, and even mobile or cellular options.

Rather than committing to a single protocol, the system would support multiple protocol stacks. At minimum, it would run both TCP/IP and OSI protocol suites on an end-to-end basis, allowing different systems to coexist and interoperate. The network would include servers for name resolution, email, database services, multicast routing, and cryptographic certificates, along with collaboration tools like video conferencing.

Experimental research facilities would be interconnected with operational NREN infrastructure, ensuring the system could evolve as technology advanced.
sections.plainLanguage: The network would use different types of cables and technologies all working together, like different highways connecting cities. It would speak multiple "languages" (protocols) so different computers could understand each other.

sections.title: Who Uses and Provides the NREN?
sections.content:
The NREN would serve a broad constituency. Users would include universities, government research labs (DOD, DOE, NASA, NIH), non-profit and for-profit R&D organizations, federally funded research centers, private enterprise, libraries, and schools at all levels. This diversity was a strength: the Internet had already proven it could accommodate academic institutions, government facilities, and commercial entities simultaneously.

Service providers would evolve over time. In the 1980s, the model relied on government-sponsored backbone networks connected to intermediate-level regional networks and local private networks. As the 1990s approached, the paper predicted a shift toward commercially operated backbone networks running at gigabit speeds, with federal support moving toward institutional vouchers rather than direct network ownership.

Vendors would supply the equipment—routers, switches, optical transmission systems, and other hardware. The NREN architecture needed to be compatible with commercial telecommunications technology and standards like SONET, ATM switches, and frame relays.
sections.plainLanguage: Schools and research centers would use the network. Phone and internet companies would operate parts of it. Equipment makers would sell the computers and routers that run it.

sections.title: Making It Work: Operations and Billing
sections.content:
A highly distributed network serving many constituencies required careful coordination. The RFC noted the parallel with the U.S. telephone system: local carriers and inter-exchange carriers (IECs) had learned to collaborate, and the NREN would need similar coordination among its many operators.

Accounting and billing were essential: the system needed to identify users and compute usage charges, though different organizations might choose different models. Some might use usage-based billing, others fixed access charges modulated by data rate, or a mix for different volume levels.

An operational forum would be needed where network operators debated policy and established methods for cooperative operation. This might build on the Internet Engineering Task Force or use existing telecommunications organizations, but ultimately would need to embrace diverse participants beyond federal sponsorship.

The paper outlined a novel idea: a voucher system where researchers could select which NREN service provider to use, with federal subsidies gradually diminishing over time. This resembled food stamps: initially high federal support would eventually fade, leaving users to make cost-based decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: Running a big network means someone has to pay for it and keep track of who uses what. The paper suggests letting researchers pick their service provider, with the government help fading over time.

sections.title: The Role of Commercial Services
sections.content:
A crucial theme throughout the RFC is the importance of commercial participation. Federal government ownership and operation of the entire NREN infrastructure was deemed unsustainable and undesirable. Instead, the paper advocated for building the NREN with commercial service provision from the start, creating a hybrid system where federal support and private enterprise both played roles.

This shift in philosophy was significant. Rather than relying on federal control and operation, the NREN could achieve "scale and ubiquity" through publicly accessible commercial facilities. Federal subsidies could focus on direct support to users—particularly research and educational institutions—rather than owning and operating network infrastructure.

The gigabit backbone components might be strictly commercial from inception, even if lower-speed components of the NREN remained a mix of private, public, and federally subsidized networks. This approach eliminated unnecessary federal control while maintaining the ability to support research and education.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of the government owning and running all the cables, private companies could build and operate much of it. The government would pay researchers and schools to use it, rather than managing the whole network itself.
